title: Cancellation Fault Injection Probe

doubleIgnoreDefinition.statement: A provider DOUBLE-IGNORES cancellation when it refuses BOTH of the gateway's cancellation mechanisms.
doubleIgnoreDefinition.refusal1_signal: It adds no 'abort' listener, never reads signal.aborted, and does not stop when CapabilityGateway calls controller.abort(). The provider is handed the signal and does not look at it.
doubleIgnoreDefinition.refusal2_deadline: Its promise never settles: no resolve, no reject, no timer. It therefore outlives timeoutMs, outlives the execute() call that started it, and is STILL IN FLIGHT when the client's retry is admitted.
doubleIgnoreDefinition.whyThisIsTheFaithfulFault: Either refusal alone is a milder, different fault. Ignoring only the signal but settling at the deadline is cancellable in effect — the gateway's Promise.race observes an outcome once the external work finishes. Hanging while honouring the signal stops the external work the moment controller.abort() fires, which is exactly what the gateway's cancel-then-reject ordering (capability-gateway.ts:200-201) was written for. Only both together leave an uncancellable external effect running while a second one is admitted. TL.json open point 2 states the fault in its own two clauses: 'ignores the passed AbortSignal' AND 'hangs beyond timeoutMs'.
doubleIgnoreDefinition.declaredInCode: DOUBLE_IGNORE_DEFINITION in packages/mcp-server/test/probes/cancellation-probe.ts, asserted by a test so it cannot silently become prose.

evidence.context: Inside the catch arm of the Promise.race between request.providerAction(controller.signal) and the timeout promise (lines 204-224). The catch cannot distinguish a provider that threw from a provider that timed out, because the timeout rejects into the same catch (line 201).
evidence.existingComment: 'No outcome was produced, so the key is free again: a failed call must stay retryable.'
evidence.whyTheCommentIsWrongForThisCase: It is true of a provider that FAILED and false of one that HUNG. Nothing was produced TO THE GATEWAY; the provider is still running and its external effect is still in flight.
evidence.implementation: SqliteCapabilityAuditRepository.release, eap-repositories.ts:723-727 — DELETE FROM capability_executions WHERE tenant_id = ? AND idempotency_key = ? AND status = 'reserved'.

idempotencyKeyReleasedOnTimeout.observedNotInferred: The probe does not read this off the source. It queries the capability_executions row for a 'reserved' status immediately after the first attempt returns and before the retry is issued (ArmObservation.keyReservedAfterFirstAttempt), and observes false on all three arms.
idempotencyKeyReleasedOnTimeout.whatCorrectBehaviourWouldBe: Neither 'release' nor 'do not release'. The gateway must distinguish a provider that FAILED (settled with a rejection — nothing is in flight, the key is genuinely safe to reuse) from one that TIMED OUT (still running, uncancellable). A settled rejection may release; a timeout should leave the key in a terminal 'abandoned' state that a retry must REFUSE, forcing a new idempotency key and an explicit reconciliation of the in-flight effect. The mutation below shows that simply not releasing eliminates the duplicate, but at the cost the existing comment guards against — a hung provider would render its key permanently unusable. This is an architectural decision, is RECORDED, and was NOT taken.

effectCountPerIdempotencyKey.method: Three arms, each with its own tenant, environment and single idempotency key. Two execute() calls per arm: attempt 1 times out, attempt 2 is the client's retry with the SAME key. The double-ignoring provider appends one record per invocation to an append-only JSONL effect-ledger FILE and PERFORMS NOTHING. Counts are read back off that file after every call returned (ADR-0021), never from an in-process counter.

arms.why: A reversible capability needs no operator approval, so once the timeout releases the reservation NOTHING stands between the retry and a second provider invocation. The idempotency key — the one control whose entire purpose is to make a retry safe — provides zero protection, and the first invocation is still running when the second starts.

The duplicate is avoided, but NOT by the idempotency key, which was released and freely re-reserved. It is avoided because the operator's grant is single-use and was consumed by the first attempt. The refusal code proves which control fired: APPROVAL_ALREADY_USED, never IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT.

The client is told PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE, whose stated obligation is 'Audit failure and retry provider when available'. The operator issues a fresh grant — the sanctioned response. That re-arms the single-use barrier, and the idempotency key does not re-arm with it. A second IRREVERSIBLE effect is admitted under the SAME idempotency key while the first is in flight.

effectCountPerIdempotencyKey.duplicateIsConcurrentNotSequential: In both duplicating arms the second invocation starts while the first has not settled (inFlight = 2). This is strictly worse than a replay: no compensating action can be ordered against an effect that has not finished.

answerToTlOpenPoint2: Releasing the idempotency key on timeout does NOT prevent duplicate execution. It is the mechanism that permits it. For a reversible capability the retry produces a second concurrent provider invocation under the same key with nothing standing in its way. For an irreversible capability the duplicate is prevented only by single-use operator approval — an authorization control with a different purpose and a different lifetime, doing an idempotency control's job — and that barrier is defeated the moment an operator legitimately re-approves in response to the PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE the client was handed.

1_effectsCountedNeverPerformed.how: The fault provider's entire body is one appendFileSync into the probe's own temporary JSONL ledger. It contacts no external system, mutates nothing outside that file, and there is no code path in the probe that could perform a real irreversible effect. The duplicate is observable without being executed.

2_deterministicAndBlocking.how: Observations are counts of discrete events, refusal codes and a reservation row — no duration, no timestamp difference, no rate. CancellationObservation carries no duration field, so a verdict cannot be a function of a timing even by accident (pinned by a test). analyzeCancellation is a pure function over the durable record and its verdict is asserted in two annotated, blocking test cases in the suite. NO Benchmark Ledger sample is recorded by this probe.
2_deterministicAndBlocking.pinnedInBothDirections: CHARACTERISED records today's effect count, refusal codes and reservation outcome per arm, each labelled SAFE or UNSAFE. analyzeCancellation refuses any departure in EITHER direction: a change that adds a third effect fails, and so does one that removes the duplicate. A safety-critical duplicate-effect property must not change without the change being stated.

foundButNotOwned.finding: PRODUCTION BEHAVIOUR IS UNSAFE. A retry after a capability timeout can produce a duplicate, CONCURRENT external effect under a single idempotency key. For reversible capabilities nothing prevents it at all. For irreversible capabilities the only barrier is single-use operator approval, which an operator legitimately re-arms in response to the PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE the client is told to retry on.
foundButNotOwned.notFixedBecause: Whether the gateway should stop releasing the key on timeout is an architectural decision with a real cost, and it is not a probe task's to take. The probe pins the behaviour so it cannot change silently; it does not bless it.
foundButNotOwned.suggestedDirection: Distinguish a settled provider rejection (safe to release) from a timeout (still in flight). Leave a timed-out key in a terminal 'abandoned' state that a retry must REFUSE, forcing a new idempotency key and explicit reconciliation of the in-flight effect.

foundButNotOwned.finding: Not releasing the key eliminates the duplicate outright — mutation M1 dropped all three arms to exactly 1 invocation. So the unsafe behaviour costs one line and buys only retryability-after-a-genuine-failure. The cost/benefit is more lopsided than the existing comment at capability-gateway.ts:211 suggests.
foundButNotOwned.notFixedBecause: Same as above — architectural, and the naive fix trades one defect for another (a hung provider permanently burns its idempotency key).

foundButNotOwned.finding: CapabilityGateway abandons the provider promise on timeout. `Promise.race` rejects and the provider's promise is never awaited again, so a provider that later rejects produces an unhandled rejection, and one that never settles is retained for the process's lifetime. The probe deliberately creates three of these per run and they are harmless here because they hold only a closure, but a real provider holding a socket or worker would leak.
foundButNotOwned.notFixedBecause: Out of scope; production code was deliberately left untouched.
